t: Monocard is a raw photo editor for cameras with a monochrome sensor. This chapter helps you install it, learn the window, and develop and export a first photo. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

System Version Processor Graphics macOS 13.4 or later Apple silicon The Mac's own Linux glibc 2.39 or later, and fontconfig 64-bit Intel or AMD A Vulkan driver Windows Windows 10 or later 64-bit Intel or AMD A driver for Vulkan or DirectX 12 The Linux and Windows versions have had little testing. Import from the camera by USB has not been tried with a camera on Linux or Windows. Some masks and some retouch tools need a model. Monocard asks before it downloads one.
Download Monocard.dmg. Open it and drag Monocard to Applications. The app is signed and notarized.

To run Monocard without an install, download the AppImage, make it executable, and run it. To install Monocard for your user, download the.tar.gz archive from the releases page, unpack it, and run./install.sh. To remove it, run./uninstall.sh.

Download the zip file and unpack it. Run bin\monocard-ui.exe. The programs are not signed, so Windows may ask before the first start. Keep the files of the bin folder together. To remove Monocard, delete the folder.

Monocard asks GitHub once a day whether there is a new version. It sends only the version number. When there is one, a line above Settings... in the left pane says so. Monocard does not install it. To turn the check off, open Settings..., choose About, and clear Check for a new version at launch.

Click Open folder... or press Ctrl+O, and choose a folder of monochrome photos. In the grid, choose a photo and press D. The camera's own preview shows first. Monocard's develop replaces it. In LOOK, click a look, for example Street. Click None to take it off. See Looks. In BASIC, move Exposure, Blacks, and Whites. Press Z to see the photo in zones, and press Z again to go back. Press A to see the photo as it was, and B to go back to your edit. Click Export... or press Ctrl+Shift+E. Choose Grey JPEG in Preset, choose a folder, and click Export. See Export. Monocard saves the edit as you work. There is no Save command. Press Ctrl+Z to undo. The first time you open a raw of a Ricoh GR IV Monochrome, a card shows some facts about the camera. Click Start to close it, or Show Highlights to open the HIGHLIGHTS panel.

Monocard never changes a photo. It keeps the edit in a file beside it: the edit of IMG_0001.DNG is in IMG_0001.DNG.mcd. When you move or back up your photos, take the.mcd files too. To keep these files in a hidden.monocard folder instead, open Settings..., choose Library, and set Edits go to Hidden folder. An edit that version 0.1.2 saved does not open in 0.1.0 or 0.1.1.

Monocard is built on Greycard, and you can install both. They share no settings and no library. Monocard reads a.gcd file of Greycard when the photo has no.mcd file. The photo opens with that edit, rating, and flag. The first save in Monocard writes an.mcd file. After that, Monocard does not read the.gcd file. Monocard never writes a.gcd file. When it moves a photo, it moves the.gcd file with it. When it deletes a photo, the.gcd file stays.

Monocard lists monochrome photos and color photos: DNG files of a monochrome sensor. A JPEG, PNG, or TIFF whose camera name says that it is monochrome, for example RICOH GR IV Monochrome. A JPEG, PNG, or TIFF with one channel. Color photos: raws of color cameras, and color JPEG, PNG, and TIFF files. Monocard shows them in grey. See Color photos. A JPEG beside a DNG of the same name goes with that DNG. To leave color photos out, turn on Hide color photos in Settings..., Editing. Monocard reads it when it starts. A raw that is not a DNG counts as color. So does a black and white photo from another camera or a scanner that is kept in three channels, and a monochrome camera's JPEG with a color tone in it, such as sepia. A camera's JPEG is already rendered by the camera. You edit it with the same panels, but some controls are for a raw only. See Develop a JPEG.

Monocard is made for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome. DNGs of other monochrome cameras open, and they have had less testing. Import from the camera by USB is new and has had little testing. The bundled profile of the GR IV Monochrome holds no measurements. Monocard uses the noise that the DNG names, or estimates it from the photo. You can measure your sensor. The learned denoise, Fast and Best, uses published models trained on photos of other cameras. A model trained on the GR IV Monochrome does not exist yet. The bundled looks Solar 1, Solar 2, and Solar 3 are not matched to the camera's Solarized modes. No look of the camera's picture modes comes with Monocard. You fit them from your own photos. Clipped light is lost. A monochrome sensor has no other channel to take it from. The text that Monocard adds to Greycard is in English only.

Click Report a problem... at the bottom of the left pane. It opens the form of Monocard in your browser, with the version, the system, and the graphics card filled in. It also opens the folder of the log. Drag monocard-ui.log into the form. Say what you did and what you expected. The logs of the three runs before are monocard-ui-1.log, the latest, to monocard-ui-3.log. System Folder of the log macOS ~/Library/Logs/monocard Linux ~/.local/state/monocard Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\monocard\logs You can also write on the issues page. Do not send them to Greycard.

The Library shows your photos as a grid. This chapter describes how to open folders, filter and sort photos, add keywords, and use collections, stacks, and archives. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

Monocard lists monochrome photos, and color photos in grey. With Hide color photos on, color photos are not listed, counted, or opened, and when a folder has no monochrome photos, the status line says so. For the exact rule, see Which photos are listed. A DNG and a JPEG with the same name in the same folder are one photo. The photo has the mark +JPEG, and one rating, flag, label, and set of keywords. To list the JPEG as its own photo, turn on Treat a JPEG beside its raw as a separate frame in Settings.

Click Open folder... at the top of the left pane, or press Ctrl+O. The name of the open folder is below the button. Click the name for the last ten folders. Library and Loupe at the top of the left pane switch between the grid and one photo. G does the same. E, Enter, or a double-click opens the photo in the Loupe, and D opens it in Develop. For all the keys, see Keys.

The Library, with the filter bar on Use the arrow keys, Home, and End to move. To select more photos, use Ctrl+click or Shift+click. Ctrl+A selects all the photos that are shown. To change the size of the tiles, drag Tile size, press + or −, or use Ctrl with the wheel. The size is from 96 to 512 pixels. Right-click a photo for its menu. A photo with an edit shows the edit and not the camera's picture. These marks are at the top right of a thumbnail: Mark Meaning Pencil The photo has an edit Picture with an arrow The photo was exported Bookmark The photo is in a collection +JPEG The camera's JPEG is with the raw Marks on the tiles, enlarged: a blue label, a bookmark, a version named Dark, and a stack of two A version has its own tile after the photo. A file that cannot be read says Unreadable.

The left pane of the Library A root is a folder that you add to your library. Monocard keeps an index of the photos in it, so that you can filter all your roots together. The roots are under ROOTS in the left pane of the grid. To add a root, click + Add a root.... To add the open folder, click + Add this folder. All roots lists every photo in your library. Right-click a root for Rename..., Use as an archive, and Remove from library. These do not change the folder on the disk. FOLDERS shows the folders inside the open root. Turn on With subfolders to show a folder with everything under it. When it is off, the folders inside the open folder are tiles above the photos. A folder on your own disk is watched, and new photos show at once. A folder on a network is read again every 10 minutes. You can change the time in Settings. When the disk of a root is not connected, the root says offline. You can still browse, filter, and cull its photos from the local previews.

The filter bar is in the header of the grid and in the CULLING section. Press Ctrl+F or / to type in it. The filter bar, enlarged, with a term typed Control What it shows Stars Photos with that rating. Click or more to change it to exactly Flag Unflagged, Pick, or Reject Label One of the five colors, or no label Camera, Lens, Day Photos with that value Kind Raw, JPEG, PNG, or TIFF Keyword Photos with that keyword ISO, Focal Photos in a range. Drag the two ends Chips of one group add to each other. Chips of different groups narrow each other. Camera, Lens, Day, ISO, and Focal show after Monocard has indexed the folder. Clear shows all the photos again. Words in the text field find photos by file name or keyword. You can also type terms: Term Example camera:, lens:, name:, folder:, keyword: camera:GR iso, focal, aperture, shutter, focus iso>=3200 rating rating>=3 date date:2026-09 flag flag:pick label label:none kind kind:raw has:versions Photos that have a version Use =,!=, <, <=, >, and >= for numbers and dates. Put a value that has a space in double quotes.
Click the arrows at the end of the filter bar. You can sort by Capture time, Name, Rating, Date edited, or Focus, in either direction. Focus is a score of how sharp the sharpest part of the photo is.

The METADATA section has Title and Keywords. It is in the left pane of the grid, and below the CULLING section in Cull. To add a keyword, type it and press Enter or a comma. To remove it, click the x on its chip. To keep a title, press Enter. Both change all the selected photos. A keyword that only some of them have is dimmed. Click it to add it to the others.

A collection is a list of photos from any folders, in an order that you choose. The photos stay where they are. Collections are under COLLECTIONS in the left pane of the grid. To make one, click + New collection.... To add photos, press B, or right-click and choose Add to collection. Press B again to take them out. On the Develop tab with a monochrome photo, B shows the photo after the edit instead. To change the order, drag photos in the grid. Right-click a collection for Rename..., Capture order, and Delete.... Delete removes the collection and not its photos. A smart collection is a saved filter. Set the filter bar, click Save..., and type a name. Its photos change as your ratings change.

A stack puts photos of one folder behind one photo. To make one, select photos and press Ctrl+G. To undo it, press Ctrl+Shift+G. To open or close it, press S in the grid, or click its badge. To put a photo on top, press Shift+S in the grid, or choose Set as top of stack in the menu. Stack bursts in the menu finds bursts and stacks each one, with its sharpest photo on top. What you do to a closed stack, such as a rating or an export, is done to its top photo only.

An archive is a root that holds the long-term copy of your photos, for example on a network drive. Right-click a root and choose Use as an archive. Back up copies the photos that are not on the archive, with their edits. Click the cloud button in the header of the grid, or right-click a photo and choose Back up to and the name of the archive. Bring back copies photos from the archive to another root. Each copy is checked, and a picture on the archive is never written over.
The edit, rating, flag, label, and keywords of a photo are in an.mcd file beside it. See Where your edits are kept. Monocard can also write an.xmp file for other programs. See Sidecars.

Monocard copies photos from a memory card, from a folder, or from a Ricoh GR IV Monochrome on a USB cable. It writes nothing on the card or the camera, and it deletes nothing there. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

h: Import from a card or folder
t: In the grid, click Import... in the left pane and choose From a card or folder..., or press Ctrl+Shift+I. Check From. Monocard fills it in when it finds a card. To choose another folder, click Choose.... Set the other rows. Click the import button, for example Import 214 frames. Row What it does To The folder that the photos go into Folders Folders to make inside To, as a pattern. Leave it empty for none Name The new file name, as a pattern. {name} keeps the camera's name Preset A preset to apply to each imported photo Backup A second folder that gets a copy of every file. Clear takes it off Verify against the card Compares photos already in To with the card, byte for byte The Import sheet The line below Name shows where the first photo goes.

DNG files of a monochrome sensor, and monochrome JPEG, PNG, and TIFF files. The camera's JPEG of a raw, with the raw's new name. An.xmp file, with the photo that it belongs to. Videos and other files stay on the card. With Hide color photos on, color photos stay on the card too.

Token Becomes {date} The day of the photo, such as 2026-09-24 {yyyy} {mm} {dd} The year, the month, and the day {name} The camera's file name, without its extension {camera} The camera model {seq} The number of the photo in this import, such as 0001 {folder} The photo's folder under From A / in Folders makes a folder in a folder, such as {yyyy}/{date}.

Each copy is read back and compared with what was read from the card. If a file fails, the import stops and names it. Run the import again to continue. A photo that you imported before is not copied again. A file is never written over: a new file with a name that is taken gets -1 after it. To stop an import, click Stop import in the left pane. The photo in hand is finished first.
To add a folder to your library without a copy, choose Add in place at the top of the sheet. The folder becomes a root.

Monocard can import from a Ricoh GR IV Monochrome on a USB cable, on a Mac, on Linux, and on Windows. Other cameras are not offered. This import has had little testing, and none with a camera on Linux or Windows. Connect the camera with a USB cable and turn it on. The camera window opens. Wait for the list. It can grow for some seconds. If photos are missing, click Read again. Set To, Folders, Name, Preset, and Backup, as for a card. Select photos and click Import selected, or click Import all. The camera window Import all leaves out the photos that are marked Imported and the ones that the window does not show. The window closes when the import ends without a fault. After a stop or a fault, it stays open and its marks show what is left. In the window What it does Show All photos, or Not imported. The window keeps your choice for the next time Sort, Tile size The order and the size of the pictures Click, Cmd+click, Shift+click, Cmd+A Select one photo, add or remove one, select a range, select all Arrow keys Go to another photo Space Selects the photo, or clears it Double-click, or Return Shows a larger picture. The arrow keys go to the next one Esc Closes the larger picture, then clears the selection, then closes the window The window opens by itself one time for each connection, but not over a sheet or a menu, or during an import or an export. To open it yourself, click Import... and choose From the camera.... To keep it closed, turn off Open the camera window when a camera is connected in Settings.

h: What is imported from the camera
t: Only DNG and JPEG files are offered. Other files stay on the camera, and the window counts them. A DNG and a JPEG with the same name in the same folder are one photo. The photos are copied to a temporary folder first, so the disk needs room for them twice. Each temporary copy must have the size that the camera gives. The import is checked against that copy and not against the camera. If you click Stop during the copy from the camera, or disconnect the camera, nothing is imported. On Linux and Windows the pictures in the window are the camera's own small thumbnails, so they look soft at a large Tile size.

Linux lets only the system open a USB device unless a udev rule allows you. If the window says that Monocard may not open the camera, install the rule that comes with Monocard, then disconnect the camera and connect it again: sudo install -m 0644 70-monocard-camera.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/ sudo udevadm control --reload-rules sudo udevadm trigger --subsystem-match=usb The file 70-monocard-camera.rules is in the unpacked tarball, beside install.sh. In the AppImage it is in usr/share/doc/monocard: run the AppImage with --appimage-extract to get it. Or make the file yourself, with this one line: SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ENV{DEVTYPE}=="usb_device", ATTR{idVendor}=="25fb", ATTR{idProduct}=="2127", TAG+="uaccess" If the window says that another program has the camera open, the file manager may have opened it. Unmount the camera there, then click Read again.

There is nothing to install. Windows installs its own driver for the camera when you connect it the first time, and Monocard uses that driver. If you replaced the driver with WinUSB (for example with Zadig), Monocard uses WinUSB. If the window says that another program has the camera open, close the Photos app or the other import program, then click Read again. Monocard does not take pictures with the camera, change its settings, delete its photos, or connect to it by Wi-Fi.

Import... > A Lightroom catalog... reads a Lightroom Classic catalog (.lrcat). Quit Lightroom first. Choose the catalog, and set the folders that were not found. Click Check and then Write. It brings ratings, flags, color labels, keywords, titles, captions, crops, virtual copies as versions, stacks, and collections, and adds the folders as roots. Tone and color settings come as a step in the history, but the develop of a monochrome photo does not use them. The import does not check whether a photo is monochrome. It writes.mcd files beside the color photos of the catalog too. A photo that you edited or rated in Monocard is left as it is, unless you turn on the switch to write over it.
To cull is to look through a shoot and to choose the photos to keep. You set flags, stars, and labels, and then you move the rejects out of the way. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

Mark Keys In the menu Stars 1 to 5. 0 clears them Rating Flag P picks, X rejects, U clears Pick, Reject, Unflag Label 6 red, 7 yellow, 8 green, 9 blue. The same key again clears it Label The menu opens with a right-click on a photo. The purple label is in the menu only. Labels keep their colors in Monocard. If you select more than one photo, a key or a menu item acts on all of them. Ctrl+Z undoes the last change of a mark, and Ctrl+Shift+Z does it again. Marks are kept in the.mcd file of the photo, with your edit. All versions of a photo share them. To find photos by their marks, use the filter bar.

Click Cull above the photo, or press C in the grid. In the Develop tab with a monochrome photo open, C shows the clip map. Click Cull there. The Cull tab The panel has these rows under CULLING: CULLING, enlarged Row What it does Picture Camera JPEG shows the camera's picture, which opens fast. Developed shows your edit Turn Turns the photo: Left or Right Show The filter bar Compare Shows 1, 2, or 4 photos. It is available with Camera JPEG Move on after a rating, flag or label Goes to the next photo after each mark. It is off at first Move N rejects... Moves the rejects of the folder Delete selection... Deletes the selected photos Delete rejects folder... Deletes the photos in the rejects folder Develop Goes to the Develop tab METADATA is below CULLING, with the title, the caption, the keywords, and the capture data.

Key What it does Space Shows the photo at 1:1, or fits it Z Shows the photo at 3:1, or fits it Shift+J Focus peaking: marks the sharpest parts V Shows two photos, four photos, or one ← → Goes to another photo Enter, D, Esc Goes to the Develop tab

Press V, or click 2 or 4 beside Compare. Monocard shows the photo and the ones next to it. The keys for stars, flags, and labels act on the photo that is chosen. Four photos compared. The frame marks the one that the keys act on To compare the versions of one photo, use Compare versions in its menu. To compare the photos of a stack, use Compare stack.

Press L to see the photos large, on a plain background. The background is the Canvas of Settings. The lightbox To show from two to six photos across, use Tile size or + and −. It starts at four. Use the arrow keys to choose a photo. The keys for stars, flags, and labels work here. Press J to show the marks on the photos. Press Enter to open the photo in the loupe. Press Esc, G, or L, or click ×, to leave.

Mark the photos with X. Click Move N rejects.... The button shows the number of them. Monocard asks Move the rejects? Click Move. The photos go to a folder named rejects in the folder of the shoot. The.mcd file, the XMP file, and the camera's JPEG go with each one. A file in rejects is never written over. Nothing is deleted. To undo the move, click Move back. The Rejects menu at the top of the grid shows how many rejects there are and has the same commands.

Press Delete (or ⌫ on a Mac), or click Delete selection... or Delete rejects folder.... Monocard asks first. Move to the trash is the default button. Delete permanently is offered only when the trash refuses the files. A permanent delete cannot be undone. The.mcd and the XMP file are deleted with the photo, and all versions of the photo go with it. A.gcd file that Greycard wrote stays.

If the camera's clock was wrong, select the photos and choose Shift capture time of… in the menu. Set Shift by, or use Set this frame to to give the correct time of one photo. The other selected photos shift by the same amount. Click Apply. Clear shift puts the camera's time back. The raw file is not changed.
The Develop tab edits the whole photo. This chapter goes through its six panels from top to bottom. To edit a part of the photo, see Masks.

Click the title of a panel, or a line with an arrow such as Levels, to fold or open it. Click the reset arrow in a title to put the panel back to what the photo started with. Drag a slider. Hold Shift to move it a tenth as far. Double-click it to put it back to its default. Click the number of a slider to type a value. Click a slider, then use the arrow keys or the mouse wheel for small steps. Every change is a step in HISTORY.
A raw with no edit starts from its camera's profile. The one for the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome sets Sharpen to Capture at 25% and turns Link to ISO on. You can also start from the camera's picture mode.

The camera already rendered a JPEG, so Monocard applies no display transform to it, and it starts as the camera made it. Display transform, and Contrast, Shoulder, and Toe under Transform, do not show. The camera profile and the hot pixel repair do not apply. If strong edits make the JPEG's 8 by 8 blocks show, use Remove JPEG blocks.

Key What it does on the Develop tab A Shows the photo before your edit B Shows your edit S Shows before and after, split, and back Z Zone view, on or off C Clip map, on or off Elsewhere, some of these keys do something else. See Keys.

The scopes stay above the tabs. Histogram shows how many pixels are at each level. Wave shows the levels across the width of the picture. Raw shows what the sensor recorded, before any edit, in stops under its clip point. Selection counts only the pixels of the chosen mask, on the Masks tab. Point at the picture to see its level, L from 0 to 255. Histogram and Wave. The white square says that the picture reaches white The numerals over Raw are zones, a stop each, with V at middle grey. The line under it says how much of the photo clipped, and how many stops its brightest light that did not clip is under the clip point. No slider changes it. A JPEG has no Raw. The squares in the corners of Histogram light when the picture reaches black or white. Click one to mark those pixels with lines. J turns both marks on or off. They show what the file clips. The clip map shows what the sensor clipped.
A look sets several controls at once. Click a tile to put it on, and None to take it off. Strength goes from 0 to 100%. See Looks. The LOOK panel. Each tile is the open photo under that look

Off when a film is set in FILM BASIC, with Transform open The display transforms, at the same settings

Monocard opens a color photo in grey. It uses Greycard's color develop with the camera's own white balance, and then mixes red, green, and blue into one grey picture. After that, every panel and every look works on it as on a monochrome photo. Filter sets the mix. None gives the lightness that the eye sees. The others work as color filters on black and white film: a filter lightens its own color and darkens the opposite one. A grey stays the same grey through every filter. Filter Use it to Yellow Darken a blue sky a little Orange Darken a blue sky more, and soften skin Red Make a blue sky almost black, and lighten red Green Lighten leaves and grass, and darken red and skin Blue Lighten a blue sky, and darken red and yellow The filters are first versions, not measured filters. With a film in FILM, the mix is the film's color sensitivity, and the filter acts on the light before the film. The grid shows a color photo's camera preview in grey without the filter until the photo has an edit.

Control Range Default What it does Contrast 0.5 to 3 1.5 The slope at middle grey Shoulder 0 to 100% 50% How softly the highlights roll off Toe 0 to 100% 50% How softly the shadows roll off White ceiling 50 to 100% 100% The light of paper white Black floor 0 to 0.1 0 The light of the deepest black

Preset sets the curve to Linear, Soft S, Strong S, Lifted, or Faded. Click the curve to add a point, up to 16. Drag a point to move it. Double-click a point to remove it. The two end points stay. The curve, with Levels open The presets of the curve The histogram is behind the curve. When the sensor clipped in the photo, a dashed line shows where its white is, and the part beyond it is hatched. Levels has Input black, Input white, Output black, and Output white, each from 0 to 100%.

FILM exposes the photo on a black and white film, develops it, and prints the negative on a darkroom paper. The film's print then takes the place of the display transform. FILM, with a split-grade print Control Range Default What it does Film None and 18 films None The film the photo is exposed on. None keeps the display transform of BASIC Development -3 to +3 0 Push (+) or pull (-). One step is about 19% more time in the developer, a push of one stop. Middle grey stays where it is Developer D-76, D-76 1+1, HC-110 B, Rodinal 1+50 D-76 Each at its own normal time. It changes the grain, the edge effect, and how the temperature and the agitation act. With a film only Bath temperature 18 to 24 °C 20 °C A warmer developer works faster: the same time gives a harder negative. With a film only Agitation Continuous, Every 30 s, Every minute, Semi-stand, Stand Every 30 s Each at its own normal time. Less agitation holds back the highlights and makes a stronger edge effect. With a film only Halation 0 to 200% 100% A soft glow around bright points, from light that bounces off the back of the film. With a film only Edge effect 0 to 200% 100% A dark and a light rim along an edge, from the developer. It makes the negative look sharper. With a film only Paper Six papers Ilford Multigrade IV RC The paper the negative is printed on. With a film only Split grade On, off Off Prints with two exposures, through filter 00 and filter 5, in place of Paper grade. On an Ilford Multigrade paper, with a film Paper grade 00 to 5 2 Changes contrast as darkroom paper does. Low grades are soft, with more greys. High grades are hard, with more black and white. With a film, it sets the paper's filter. Without one, middle grey, black, and white stay where they are. It works the same on a raw and on a JPEG Soft (00), Hard (5) -3 to +3 EV 0 The two exposures of a split-grade print, in stops of time (EV). Shown in place of Paper grade Process Silver gelatin, Lith, Cyanotype Silver gelatin How the print is made. Lith and cyanotype work with or without a film Overexposure 0 to 4 EV 0 Lith and cyanotype: exposure over the normal print. Lith printers often give 2 to 3 stops Snatch, Abruptness 0 to 100% 55%, 60% Lith: how early the shadows go black, and how suddenly Sensitizer Classic, New Classic Cyanotype: Herschel's formula, or Mike Ware's, which holds a deeper blue Range 0.5 to 3 1.4 Cyanotype: the density range the sensitizer holds. Lower is harder Bleach, Tannin 0 to 100% 0% Cyanotype: washing soda clears the blue from the highlights; tannin turns what is left brown The films are Kodak Tri-X 400, T-Max 100, T-Max 400, T-Max P3200, Plus-X 125 and Double-X 5222; Ilford HP5 Plus, FP4 Plus, Pan F Plus 50, Delta 100, Delta 400, Delta 3200, SFX 200, XP2 Super and Ortho Plus 80; and Fujifilm Acros II, Neopan 400 and Neopan 1600. Each film is its characteristic curve, from the maker's data sheet: how dark the negative gets for each amount of light. A film with a long toe, such as Tri-X, keeps more shadow detail. A film with a short one, such as Pan F Plus, makes deeper blacks. Eight films develop as their data sheets show: Kodak Tri-X 400, T-Max 100 and T-Max 400, from Kodak's curves at several times in D-76, and Ilford HP5 Plus, FP4 Plus, Delta 100, Delta 400 and Delta 3200, from Ilford's curve. On these, a longer time raises the highlights much more than the shadows and gains some speed, as a real push does. On the other ten films, Development makes the negative's contrast higher or lower by a fixed step. The papers are Ilford Multigrade IV RC, Multigrade FB Classic and Multigrade Warmtone, Kodak Polymax II RC and Polycontrast IV RC, and Foma Fomatone. Each grade is timed so that middle grey prints the same. FB Classic has a deeper black than the RC paper. Polycontrast IV has grades 1 to 5 only; a lower grade prints as 1. On Multigrade Warmtone and Fomatone the silver is warm, so the photo is toned and exports in color. In a split-grade print, the soft exposure prints the light tones and the hard exposure fills the shadows. At 0 and 0 the print matches grade 2 at middle grey and two stops under it. Give more Soft (00) to darken the light tones, and more Hard (5) to darken the shadows. A lith print has creamy, low-contrast highlights set by the exposure, and shadows that turn black past a point set by Snatch. Its color follows the paper: warm on Fomatone, nearly neutral on the others. A cyanotype is Prussian blue and never goes black. Paper white stays white in both. Both are toned photos. A color photo goes to grey through the film's own color sensitivity, and through the Filter of BASIC. So Ortho Plus 80, which does not see red, makes red lips and red bricks dark. A monochrome photo has no color, so this does not change it. The film also sets the grain. A fast film, such as Delta 3200, has large grain. A slow one, such as Pan F Plus, has fine grain. Monocard renders the negative's silver grains at the size that matches each film's published granularity, on a 35 mm frame across the photo, so the grain has the same size in the print whether the file is small or large. A crop enlarges the grain with the picture, as it would on film. The grain is weak in the print's shadows, strongest in the midtones and light tones, and none in the paper's white. In Grain, Amount scales it and Size makes the grains smaller or larger than the film's (30% is the film's own). Roughness and Link to ISO are hidden with a film. The film's print, grain, halation and edge effect are the same on the screen and in an export. The curves were digitized from the makers' data sheets by SpektraLab (Hanze Qiu), under CC BY-SA 4.0. The film model is ported from spektrafilm (Andrea Volpato). The development, the fitted curves, and the Kodak papers are from film-darkroom (James Huckle); Multigrade Warmtone from film_tests (Rafal Lukawiecki); FB Classic, Fomatone, lith, cyanotype, and the toners from NegPy; the split-grade print from mimizan (Dragan Bojovic).

A look sets several controls of the Develop tab at once. This chapter covers the bundled looks, your own looks, the picture modes of a Ricoh GR, and recipes.

Click a tile in the LOOK panel. Each tile shows the open photo under that look. A look replaces the one before it. None takes it off and puts its controls back. Strength fades the look, from 0 to 100%. The controls hold the values of the look, so you can change any of them afterward. Look What it does Street Neutral, full tonal range, a gentle shoulder Hard Deep blacks, strong midtone contrast, fine grain Soft Print Lifted blacks, paper white at 0.94, low contrast Night Push Pushed film, for ISO 12800 and up, with denoise and grain Solar 1, Solar 2, Solar 3 Tone reversed about the middle, at both ends, or in the shadows Selenium A cool tone in the shadows only Warm Fibre A warm paper tone across the picture High Key Bright, few true blacks The ten looks on one photo Solar 1 to 3 are not matched to the camera's Solarized modes. Selenium and Warm Fibre tone the photo, so it exports in color.

Twelve more looks are black and white film emulations from t3mujinpack by João Almeida (MIT), named with (t3mujinpack) after the film: AGFA APX 25 and 100, Fuji Neopan 1600 and Neopan Acros 100, Ilford Delta 100, 400 and 3200, FP4 125, HP5 Plus 400 and XP2, Kodak T-Max 3200 and Tri-X 400. Each one sets the curve to the film's tone and the filter to the film's mix of colors to grey. The mix acts on color photos only. On a photo from a monochrome camera only the curve acts. The Filter row shows From LUT; choose a filter to take the film's mix off. These looks are not the films of the FILM panel, which model the film's chemistry from its data sheet.

Set the controls of the panels. A film and its settings are kept too. Click Save as look, type a name, and click Save. The look holds each control that is not at its default, Exposure too. It does not hold the crop, the lens, the masks, or the retouch. A name of your own that is in use is written over. A name of a bundled look is refused. With a look on, Export shows four buttons: Button What it writes Look The look's own file (.toml) 1D LUT A 1D.cube of 4096 entries, for grey pictures: the look's tone, and its toning as one curve a channel 3D LUT A 3D.cube of 33 points, for color pictures: the filter or film's conversion to grey, the tone, and the toning Lightroom A creative profile (-profile.xmp) and a Develop preset (-preset.xmp) Both LUTs take and give display-referred sRGB. They hold the tone and the toning only: the grain, the vignette, and the local contrast are not in a LUT. The Lightroom profile converts to black and white and holds the look's conversion and tone as a table, which Lightroom's Amount slider scales. Put it in Camera Raw's Settings folder, then restart Lightroom. The preset puts the profile on, with the clarity, texture, grain, vignette, and toning (as split toning). Import it in Lightroom's Presets panel. Lightroom's sliders are not Monocard's, so the grain and vignette look different. For your own looks, there are also Rename and Delete. Photos that have a renamed or deleted look keep their values, but Strength no longer works on them. The open photo follows a rename.

h: Import a look, a Lightroom preset, or a LUT
t: Click Import look, preset, or LUT and choose a file: A look (.toml). A monochrome Lightroom preset (.xmp). Monocard takes the basic tone, the curves, clarity, texture, grain, split toning, and vignette. A line under the button lists what it left out, such as color values and masks. The picture is not equal to Lightroom's. A LUT: a.cube (1D or 3D) or a HaldCLUT.png, made for display-referred sRGB. The look takes the file's name. A name that is in use is refused. On a grey photo a 3D LUT acts only along its black-to-white line. So the look holds that line as an editable curve, and the difference between the LUT's channels on it as toning. The LUT's filter part, how it turns colors into greys, acts on color photos only: When a filter mix comes near the LUT, the look sets the Filter to that mix. The line under the button gives how near, in levels of 255. When none does (on average more than 1.5 levels off, or 4 levels for 95% of the colors), the line says so, and the look keeps the LUT's own conversion to grey in place of a filter. In both cases the Filter row shows From LUT. The curve is fitted under the default display transform, as for a raw. A camera JPEG has no display transform, so on a JPEG the look's tone differs from the LUT's.

A look is a text file in TOML format. Monocard reads this folder when it starts: System Folder macOS ~/Library/Application Support/monocard/looks-mono Linux ~/.config/monocard/looks-mono Windows %APPDATA%\monocard\looks-mono A file names only the values that it sets: name = "My look" description = "Soft, with grain." [tools.display] contrast = 1.3 white_ceiling = 0.95 [tools.grain] amount = 0.25 To see the names of the sections and values, save a look and open its file. A control that shows a percentage is 0 to 1 in the file. A number out of range is set to the nearest end. A file with an unknown name is refused.

A Ricoh GR IV Monochrome writes its picture mode in each file. Ricoh calls it Image Control. The mode changes the JPEG only, and not the DNG. Monocard can fit a look of a mode from pairs of a DNG and its JPEG. No such look comes with Monocard. Yours show under Camera modes in the LOOK panel when a raw of that camera is open, and not for a JPEG.

These results come from one camera and two photos of the test chart. Standard and Solid also use one scene. The error is the mean, in levels of 255. Mode Result Error What is missing Standard Good 0.26 The last stop before white Solid Good 0.39 The same Solarized 1 Good 0.41 The same Solarized 2 Good, close to the limit 1.29 The same Solarized 3 Good 0.66 The same Soft Draft 1.02 Local contrast High Contrast Draft 1.49 Grain. The cause of the rest is not known HDR Tone Draft 4.81 It is local, so a curve is only near it Grainy Missing Photos The fit finds the tone curve only. Grain, sharpening, vignette, and toning are not fitted.

h: Fit a mode from your photos
t: On the camera, set every parameter of the modes to its default. Turn off Highlight Correction, Shadow Correction, noise reduction, and Peripheral Illumination Correction. Shoot RAW+JPEG in Standard, or develop one DNG in the camera in each mode. The Solarized modes need a Standard JPEG of the same DNG. Copy the DNGs and the JPEGs to a folder. Do not edit them. Open Settings... and choose Camera profiles. Under PHOTOS FOR THE FIT, click Add folder.... Subfolders are not read, and nothing is written in the folder. Click Fit all. A report says which files were left out, and why. The CAMERA MODES table shows each mode: Settings..., Camera profiles State Meaning Good Fitted, and the error is in the limits, in levels of 255: mean 1.5, 95% of the blocks at 4 or less, largest 8 Draft Fitted, and the error is over the limits. You can use it, and its tile says draft Adjusted You changed the look by hand Missing There is no fit Click a row for Use, Adjust, Export, Delete, and Fit or Fit again. Adjust puts the look on the open photo. Change the controls, then save the look under the same name. Fit all does not write over an adjusted look.
Under TEST CHART, Test chart fills the screen with 40 grey steps over 10 stops. Save chart... saves it as a picture. The page says how to photograph it.

A raw with no edit starts from the look of its camera's mode, so it opens as the camera's JPEG shows it. To start from no look, turn off Start from the camera's mode in Settings..., Editing. The setting is on by default. The photo's own settings, such as Key and Contrast, then go over the look. A photo shot at the mode's defaults gets nothing more. Each setting moves one tool: Key moves Exposure, and Contrast moves Contrast. The size of each step is a first guess for now. Toning, grain, and HDR Tone level are not put on yet.

Take flat frames, evenly lit, and dark frames, with the lens cap on, a few at each ISO. Dark frames of one second or longer are for hot pixels. In Settings..., Camera profiles, click Measure sensor noise.... Choose the folder of the frames. A report shows the result. Monocard keeps the profile in the cameras folder beside looks-mono, and uses it from the next develop. No look changes.

A recipe is the picture settings of the Ricoh GR IV Monochrome: a mode of Image Control and its parameters. Monocard keeps recipes to look at, compare, and set on the camera. A recipe does not change a photo or the camera. To develop a raw like a mode, use a look. To open the book, go to the grid, click Import... in the left pane, and choose Recipes.... Button What it does From this photo Makes a recipe from the settings that the open photo records. If the book has a recipe with the same settings, Monocard chooses that one New Makes a recipe of Standard with the default settings Import... Adds a recipe from a.toml file. A name that is in use is refused Compare with Shows the values of a second recipe. Rows with another value say Differs Duplicate, Export..., Delete Copies the recipe, writes it to a file in a folder, or deletes it Copy as text Puts the settings on the clipboard as plain text The rows are in the order of the camera's menu. A recipe has only the settings of its mode. When you choose another Mode, the settings that both modes have keep their values, and the others take their defaults. Changes are saved as you make them. To use a recipe, set its values on the camera in Image Control, then save them in Custom 1 to 3. The notes of a recipe from a photo start with the ISO, and with the red filter if it was on. What is not certain: Ricoh does not publish which mode has which setting, the ranges, or the defaults. Monocard uses what others report. The names of the tonings and of the HDR Tone levels are reported too. No photo with a toning, or with a level other than High, was seen. The meaning of the recorded grain is known in part. Recorded and two numbers, or Grainy default, is what the photo says. If you choose a size, that value is replaced. Each recipe is a file in the recipes folder beside looks-mono. A setting out of range is set to the nearest end. A file with an unknown mode, toning, or level is refused.
A mask limits an edit to a part of the photo. You make masks on the Masks tab. The edit on the Develop tab stays under all of them.

ADJUSTMENTS at the top of the tab holds Global and your masks. Click a row to choose it. The list of masks New mask adds an empty mask. A photo can have up to 16. The dot of a row switches the mask on or off. The bin of the chosen row deletes it. Right-click a mask for Duplicate mask, Copy mask, Copy masks, and Paste mask. The next drag places it Shift+M The same with a Radial shape O Shows or hides the chosen mask Esc Puts the drawing tool down One mask on the wet street and one on the doorway

Monocard asks before it downloads a model, and the sheet names the model and its size. The models that are there, and what they need, are in Settings..., Models. See Settings. The models work on a grey copy of your photo. The photo does not leave your computer.

These tools act only where the mask is. Control Range Default What it does Exposure -4 to +4 EV 0 Lightens or darkens Local contrast -100 to +100 0 Changes local contrast Zones -2 to +2 EV each 0 The nine sliders of LIGHT, -8 EV to 0 EV Curve and levels Preset, the curve, and the levels, as in BASIC MASK TOOLS, with Zones and Curve and levels open The reset arrow puts the tools back and leaves the shapes. Crop and straighten a photo, correct the lens, and remove dust and unwanted things. Crop and retouch are part of the edit and can be undone. They are never copied to other photos by Sync. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

Click the Retouch tab. Choose Heal, Clone, or Fill, and then work on the photo. Tool What it does Heal Copies another part of the photo and matches its brightness Clone Copies another part of the photo as it is Fill Removes a thing and makes a new picture in its place Control Range Start Size 0.2 to 30% 2% Feather 0 to 100% 30% Opacity 0 to 100% 100% Use the wheel or [ and ] to change the size, Shift+[ and Shift+] for the feather, and Ctrl+[ and Ctrl+] for the opacity. RETOUCH, with two repairs For Heal and Clone, Monocard chooses the part to copy from. To change it, choose the repair in the list with the tool in hand. Two pins show the repair and its source. Drag them.

Choose Fill and one of the three kinds. Paint over the thing to remove, in one or more strokes. Strokes that touch become one fill. Press Enter or click Generate. Esc drops the strokes. Kind What it does Download Patch Fills from the picture around it About 210 MB Fast Makes a new picture in four steps. It is rougher on large areas 5.5 GB, and 390 MB more Best Makes a new picture in full. It takes longer 5.5 GB Monocard asks before it downloads a model and shows its license. After that, everything runs on your computer and no photo is sent. Fast and Best need a graphics card that Monocard can use, with at least 6.3 GiB of memory if it is a separate card. Without one, they are not available. On a fill that Fast or Best made, Another makes a different result. Fill works on monochrome photos. The result is grey.

Use presets and Sync to put an edit on other photos. Use the history, snapshots, and versions to keep and compare edits of one photo. In the Develop tab, the left pane has NAVIGATOR, PRESETS, SNAPSHOTS, and HISTORY. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

Press Ctrl+Z to undo a step, and Ctrl+Shift+Z or Ctrl+Y to redo it. Press \ to see the photo as it was before the edit. To remove all of the edit, choose Reset to Original in the photo's menu. You can undo this too.

HISTORY lists the steps of your edit, such as "Exposure +0.50 EV", "Look: Street", or "Preset: Soft". It keeps the last 50 steps and Original. An export adds a row too. The left pane of Develop Hold the pointer over a step to see it on the photo. Click it to go back to it. The steps after it stay until you change something. Reset to Original puts the photo back to the start. The history is kept with the edit, so it is there the next time that you open the photo.

A snapshot is a state of the edit that you keep by name. Click Take under SNAPSHOTS. Type a name and press Enter. Hold the pointer over a snapshot to see it on the photo. Each one has buttons to restore it, rename it, and remove it. To restore a snapshot is a step that you can undo.

A version is a second edit of the same photo file. The photo is shown one time for each version. In the photo's menu What it does New version (Ctrl+') Makes a version that starts from this edit New version from the original Makes a version with no edit Rename version... Changes its name Swap with the original Makes this version the photo's own edit, and the other one the version Delete version... Asks, and then deletes this version. It cannot be undone Compare versions Shows the versions side by side in the Cull tab All versions are in the same.mcd file. They share the stars, the flag, the label, and the keywords. An export of a version has the name of the version, such as IMG_0001-Name.jpg.

In Sync settings, check what to copy. Click Apply. Everything but the masks is checked at first. You can check a whole section or its parts. To sync at once with no sheet, middle-click the sync button or a photo.
On one photo, press Ctrl+C, or choose Copy settings in its menu. Select other photos, and press Ctrl+V, or choose Paste settings. Check what to paste and click Paste.
A preset is an edit, or a part of one, that you keep to use on other photos. Monocard has no presets of its own. A preset is different from a look: a preset can also hold a lens correction and masks.

Click Save... under PRESETS. Type a Name. Check the parts to keep. The parts that differ from the defaults are checked. Click Save. Click a preset to apply it to the selected photos. It is one step in the history. It replaces the parts that it holds and leaves the rest of the edit. A preset can also be applied on import.

Click the star to make a preset a favorite. Favorites are at the top of the list too. Right-click a preset to use Move to group or Remove from group. New group... makes a group. Right-click the name of a group to use Rename group.... Click the bin, Remove, to delete a preset.

Import... under PRESETS takes.gcp files, which is the format of Monocard and Greycard presets. Presets that have only color settings are not listed. To import a Lightroom preset, see Looks. Presets are.gcp files in the presets folder. Settings says where it is.

Monocard merges some photos of one scene into one new DNG. The new DNG is monochrome, is listed like your other photos, and opens for editing. The source photos are not changed. On a Mac, use Cmd where this guide says Ctrl.

Command Photos to take Result Merge to HDR One view, with different exposures Detail in the bright and the dark parts Merge burst One view, at one exposure, shot by hand Less noise, for night and high ISO Merge to Panorama Views that overlap One wide picture Merge to Focus stack One view, with the focus at different distances One picture that is sharp from near to far All four take DNG files of a monochrome sensor. A JPEG, PNG, or TIFF is refused, because it is not a raw file. The panorama and the focus stack have had little testing with monochrome photos.

Select two or more photos in the grid or the filmstrip. Right-click one and choose a merge command. Wait. The status line shows the progress. At the end, the status line says "merged N frames into NAME". If the merge is refused, it says "not merged" and gives the reason. You can also click Merge brackets under HIGHLIGHTS in the Develop tab. It merges the two to five photos that you selected in the filmstrip to HDR. Merge burst under DETAIL merges the two to sixteen photos that you selected in the filmstrip as a burst.

Take from two to five photos with different shutter speeds and the same aperture and focus. Use a tripod if you can. Small moves between the photos are corrected. The photo in the middle of the exposures is the base. Its edit is used for the new DNG, with the exposure at 0. The sensor data of the photos is combined, before the tone controls. Brighter photos give the shadows, and darker photos give the highlights. A thing that moves between the photos is taken from one of them. The merge is refused if: The photos are of two cameras or two sizes. A photo does not state its exposure. The exposures are too far apart. A merge of more than five photos works in a different way, and has had less testing.

Take from two to sixteen photos of one view, one after the other, with the same shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. Hold the camera as still as you can; a tripod is not needed. Eight photos have about the noise of one photo at an ISO three stops lower, with the blur of one shutter speed. The photo in the middle of the selection is the reference. Its edit is used for the new DNG, with its exposure. The other photos are aligned to it: the whole photo first, then each small area of it. The sensor data is combined before the tone controls. Where a photo differs from the reference by more than its noise, for example a person who walked through, the reference is used there. The noise reduction in the Develop tab still works on the new DNG. It knows that the new DNG has less noise, so it does less. The merge is refused if: The photos are of two cameras or two sizes. The exposures differ by more than a third of a stop. Use Merge to HDR for photos at different exposures. Fewer than two or more than sixteen photos are selected.

Take the photos in order, from one side to the other, with one focal length. Let each one overlap the next one. The distortion of the lens is corrected before the merge, if there is a lens profile. The result is cut to the largest rectangle that has no empty edge. The result has at most 100 megapixels. The photo in the middle of the turn gives the view and the edit. Its exposure, lens corrections, crop, retouch, and masks are left out.

Keep the camera still, and change only the focus from one photo to the next. Select the photos in focus order, of one camera and one size. The photo in the middle gives the position and the edit, with its exposure. The other photos are aligned to it. A photo that cannot be aligned is left out, and the log says which and why. Each part of the picture comes from the photo in which it is sharpest. If there is not enough free memory, the merge is refused. Close other programs and try again.

The new file is beside the first of the photos. Merge Name HDR IMG_0001-HDR.dng Burst IMG_0001-burst.dng Panorama IMG_0001-pano.dng Focus stack IMG_0001 stack.dng If the name is taken, a number is added. A file is never written over. If the photos are in one folder, and you are not in a collection, the new photo and its sources become a stack with the new photo on top.
The monocard program has the same merges, except the burst merge, with more options. See Command line.

JPEG XL is lossy, and smaller than a JPEG of the same quality. An untoned photo is one grey channel in the file, with its profile and metadata. JPEG XL 16-bit is lossless. It holds the picture on sRGB's curve, with no profile and no metadata: the Profile, Embed profile, and Metadata rows do nothing. An untoned photo is one grey channel. Ultra HDR is a JPEG with a gain map. A viewer without HDR shows the JPEG, which is the same as a JPEG export. A viewer with HDR, such as Chrome or an Android phone on an HDR screen, uses the gain map to show the lights brighter, up to 2 stops over the JPEG's white. The shadows and the mid greys stay the same. The gain map is one grey channel, so a toned photo keeps its tint in the lights. With AgX, a film in FILM, or a camera JPEG, the HDR picture is the same as the JPEG. A watermark is not in the gain map. Not every app opens JPEG XL. Check before you send one.

Choose Text and type a line in White or Black, or choose Image and a PNG file. Click a square of the grid to place it. Size goes from 1 to 50% of the long edge, Margin from 0 to 10%, and Opacity from 5 to 100%. In a grey file, the mark is grey.

Click White, light grey, dark grey, Black, or Match. Match is the mean tone of the picture. Width goes from 0.5 to 25% of the long edge. The border is added outside the picture, so the file is larger. The window does not show it.

The monocard program does the work of Monocard from a terminal or a script. It reads the same edits, looks, presets, settings, and library as the window. Run monocard --help or monocard SUBCOMMAND --help for all the options.

System Path macOS /Applications/Monocard.app/Contents/MacOS/monocard Linux, archive bin/monocard in the folder that you unpacked Linux, AppImage Run the AppImage with --cli before the subcommand Windows bin\monocard.exe Every subcommand takes -h for help and -v for more messages. monocard -V prints the version. Color photos develop in grey, as in the window. With Hide color photos on, they are refused.

Command What it prints monocard info FILE What the file says about itself monocard route FILES... mono or color for each file monocard mode FILE... The picture mode that a Ricoh GR recorded in each DNG or JPEG

monocard export IMG_0001.DNG IMG_0001.jpg monocard export --all ~/Photos/shoot ~/Photos/out/ monocard export --look Street --long-edge 2048 IMG_0001.DNG street.jpg Each photo is written with its own edit, as the export sheet does it. The last path is the file to write, or a folder. A folder that is not there yet must end with a slash. Option What it does --all Every photo of the folders --also ROWS More rows of the folder, from 0, with commas --preset NAME Puts this preset on the edit first, as a step in its history --export-preset NAME Uses this export preset --long-edge PX The long edge, in pixels. It never enlarges --on-exists WHAT increment, overwrite, or skip, for a file that is there already --version-name NAME Exports this version --exposure EV Exposure in stops, for this run only --look NAME This look, for this run only --author NAME, --copyright TEXT Text to write in the files --no-sidecars Does not read or write the.mcd files --sidecar-folder Writes the edits to the hidden.monocard folder --xmp-sidecars Also writes.xmp files --cpu Does not use the graphics card Exit status Meaning 0 All photos were written as their edits ask 1 A photo was not written 2 Something that an edit names, such as a look, was missing, and the photo was written without it

Imports presets monocard presets --apply NAME FILES... Puts a preset on the edits of the files

Fits the picture modes as looks, from DNGs and the camera's JPEGs monocard profile build FOLDER Fits the noise profile of a camera from flat, dark, and test photos profile modes takes --out DIR, --replace, --replace-adjusted to write over looks that you changed by hand, and --dry-run to write nothing. profile build takes --out FILE.toml and --replace. The folders in a folder are not read.
